summary: This document defines a reference path for large-scale measurement of broadband access performance and measurement points for commonly used metrics. It provides an efficient way to describe where a measurement was made.

eli5.summary: When measuring how fast your Internet is, it matters where you measured. This RFC draws a map with named spots along the way.

questions: what is a lmap reference path
where do you measure broadband performance
subtitle: A common vocabulary for where to measure broadband performance

tldr.problem: When measuring broadband speed and quality, measuring different parts of the path gives different results. Networks need a standard way to describe exactly where a measurement was taken.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a generic reference path from subscriber to destination, identifying key components like the service demarcation point and transit networks. It establishes a numbered measurement point system (mpXnn) so any measurement can be described unambiguously.
tldr.outcome: LMAP and similar measurement projects can now compare results confidently because they measure equivalent points. The reference path is technology-independent, applying to DSL, cellular, fiber, and wireless.

today: RFC 7398 is the standard reference for describing where broadband measurements occur. It is used by LMAP implementations and broadband performance measurement systems worldwide.

sections.title: Why a Reference Path Matters
sections.content:
Broadband performance measurements must describe exactly where they were taken. A speed test at your home modem measures something different from a test at your Internet service provider's gateway. Without a standard framework, measurements made by different organizations are incomparable and potentially misleading.

This RFC builds on earlier IPPM (IP Performance Metrics) work to define a common reference path that applies to any network technology: DSL, 3G cellular, fiber, WiFi, and more. It establishes a universal vocabulary for describing measurement locations so that the same metric measured at equivalent points produces results that can be fairly compared.
sections.eli5: Internet speed depends on where you measure it. This RFC defines landmark points along the path so different companies measure the same spot and can fairly compare results.

sections.title: The Reference Path Model
sections.content:
The reference path divides the network into functional components. Starting from the subscriber's device, the path goes through private networks owned by the subscriber, crosses the service demarcation point (where the service provider's responsibility begins), passes through the service provider's access network with an Intra IP Access point, reaches a GRA Gateway (where globally routable IP addresses are used), crosses any intermediate transit networks with their own gateways, and finally reaches the destination host.

Components on the path are classified as dedicated (allocated only to one subscriber's traffic) or shared (serving multiple subscribers). A resource transition point marks where the path shifts from dedicated to shared components. The service demarcation point always separates the service provider's managed sub-path from the unmanaged portion beyond their control (private networks, other providers, unlicensed wireless).
sections.eli5: The path is like a journey: start at your device, go through your home network, cross into your ISP's network at a marked point, then through the ISP to the wider Internet, then to the destination. Measurement points sit at key landmarks along this journey.

sections.title: The Measurement Point Numbering System
sections.content:
Each measurement point receives a unique designation mpXnn. The X is the network number: 0 for the subscriber's home network, 1-7 for intermediate transit networks, 8 for the destination service provider network, and 9 for the destination host network. The nn component is a local number within each network: 00 for the subscriber's device or gateway, 90 for the far gateway of a network, 50 for intermediate points like a NAT, and other numbers for specific components like traffic aggregation points (20 for a DSLAM).

With this scheme, mp000 is always the subscriber's device, mp100 is the service demarcation point in the access network, mp190 is the access network gateway, mp200 is the first transit network gateway, and mp900 is the destination host. When communicating results, the measuring organization MUST provide a diagram showing the reference path, the measurement point numbers, and technology-specific details of any non-standard points.
sections.eli5: Each landmark gets a code: mpXnn. The first digit X is which network (0 for home, 1-7 for in-between, 8-9 for destination). The second two digits nn say where in that network: 00 for the near end, 90 for the far end.

sections.title: Applying the Reference Path to Real Technologies
sections.content:
The reference path maps to any network technology. For DSL, the subscriber's device connects via private networks to Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) with a modem at the service demarcation point (mp100). The BRAS (Broadband Remote Access Server) is the GRA gateway (mp190). For 3G cellular, the User Equipment (UE) is the subscriber device (mp000), the Radio Access Network and GGSN gateway form the managed sub-path, and the GGSN is the GRA gateway (mp190).

A common modern configuration uses a home router with WiFi as the CPE, a private address space internally, and a Carrier Grade NAT (CGN) deep in the service provider's network. In this case, mp100 is at the modem, the CGN's egress side is mp150 (an intermediate measurement point), and mp190 is the access network gateway. The flexibility of the reference path allows organizations to identify technology-specific measurement points while staying aligned with the standard model.
sections.eli5: Different technologies (DSL, cellular, fiber) have different devices and gear, but they all fit the same reference path. A modem in DSL maps to a user equipment in cellular; the path structure is the same.

sections.title: Scope and Practical Considerations
sections.content:
The reference path applies to both IPv4 and IPv6, though conversions between address families must be noted. When private address spaces are used throughout an access architecture, measurement points must use compatible address spaces so tests between them assess real performance. If the number of intermediate transit networks is unknown or changes over time, this must be indicated on the reference path diagram and results must be treated with caution.

The measuring organization SHOULD use consistent numbering for the same device role across all paths and SHOULD coordinate numbering with other organizations using similar technologies. Measurement point numbers SHOULD remain stable for the duration of a measurement study. The assignment can have gaps or be non-monotonic over time due to network growth, consolidation, or ownership changes; these circumstances must be documented on the reference path diagram.
sections.eli5: The numbering system is flexible enough for any network, but measurement organizations should use consistent numbers for the same device types and document any changes.
